The quijada (jawbone) is an idiophone percussion instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.211, made from the jawbone of a donkey, horse, mule or ox, whose teeth come loose as it dries and rattle like a jingler. The player holds one end and strikes the other with a hand or a stick, so that the teeth knock against the bone and give a loud sound of no fixed pitch; the stick can also be drawn along the teeth. It is popular in Mexico, Peru, El Salvador, Ecuador, Cuba and other parts of Latin America, and it appeared in early American minstrel shows; it is linked to the Africans brought to the Americas in the colonial period, and is thought to have reached Peru first, where it is used in Afro-Peruvian ensembles, in candombe, in son jarocho and similar settings, the donkey jawbone being common at carnival and religious festivals.

演奏者一手握住頜骨鼓一端，另一手以鼓棒或手掌敲擊另一端，使鬆動牙齒撞擊骨頭，發出: The player holds one end of the jawbone with one hand and strikes the other end with a drumstick or the palm, so that the loose teeth knock against the bone and give a loud sound of no fixed pitch; the stick can also be dragged along the teeth for a scraping effect. A beginner can first check that the teeth have loosened as they dried, then practise combining strokes and drags in rhythm. The sources offer no teaching material, so none is added here.
頜骨鼓為體鳴樂器，主要發聲體是驢、馬、騾或牛的頜骨，骨上牙齒經清潔組織與乾燥後鬆: The jawbone is an idiophone: its main sound source is the jawbone of a donkey, horse, mule or ox, and the teeth loosen after the tissue is cleaned off and the bone dries, so that they knock together when struck or dragged. You can strike the other end with the hand or with a stick, and the stick can be dragged along the teeth; the sources do not record the material of the stick. Apart from the animal jawbone and teeth, no other materials are recorded.
頜骨鼓發出的聲音具有獨特的嗡鳴質感，帶有粗糲而原始的音色特徵。其音域位於中低頻段: The jawbone has a distinctive buzzing quality, with a coarse and raw timbre. Its range lies in the low middle frequencies, and its volume is strong enough to carry through a band. The rattle of the loose teeth knocking together gives the sound a clearly grainy rhythmic texture, unlike the dull weight of a drum and unlike the sharp brightness of a metal instrument. The resonance comes mainly from the natural resonance of the cavity of the lower jaw, and the timbre is warm yet a little weathered. Compared with the triangle it is thicker and more rustic; compared with the bongos it has more of an eerie buzz. This distinctive sound has made it a rhythm instrument with no real substitute in Latin music, adding a local flavour and a sense of groove.
頜骨鼓被認為源自殖民時期被帶到美洲的非洲人，並先在秘魯出現，成為非裔秘魯音樂的重: The jawbone is thought to come from the Africans brought to the Americas in the colonial period; it appeared first in Peru and became an important instrument of Afro-Peruvian music. It blends African and indigenous cultures and later spread through most of Latin America, including Mexico, Peru, El Salvador, Ecuador and Cuba. In Afro-Peruvian ensembles it often carries the main rhythm, and it also appears in Argentine candombe, in Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Belizean brukdown, Mexican son jarocho and the 'costeño' ensemble; in one song from Oaxaca it keeps the beat. The donkey-jawbone version is mostly used at carnival and religious festivals, and early American minstrel shows used it too.
頜骨鼓見於拉丁美洲多地音樂，包括秘魯、墨西哥、薩爾瓦多、厄瓜多與古巴，也曾在早期: The jawbone appears in music across Latin America, including Peru, Mexico, El Salvador, Ecuador and Cuba, and it once appeared in early American minstrel shows. It is often used in Afro-Peruvian bands, in Argentine candombe, in Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Belizean brukdown, Mexican son jarocho and the 'costeño' ensemble; in songs from Oaxaca it can keep the beat, and the donkey-jawbone version is mostly seen at carnival and religious festivals.
